title: What Changes at Each Scale: From First Store to Group
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/43-commerce-scaling-stages/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (a thesis paragraph, a roadmap and a conclusion paragraph that answers the opening); two Group-stage paragraphs that made one point are merged. These are recorded in decision_log.

know: The four stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group) as shapes of channels and stock locations, with revenue bands as rough markers only, and the map of what is typical and what becomes necessary at each: where the order and stock truth live, product data, fulfillment, finance, integration style, who builds and runs, fees met, peak day, decisions due and failure patterns.

How fresh each fact must be at each stage, the Group stage's share-or-separate table per capability, and the transition signals (a fee cliff, a second stock location, a retail chain asking for EDI, two order counts, a connector without an owner, support opening several systems, an app writing a fact another system owns, a first peak-day integration failure, a second brand).

Kestrel & Pine's path priced: Starting 2016–2018, Growing 2019–2022, Omnichannel since 2023; the April 2027 stage map, which maps its thirteen systems to their stages, attributes eight of its ten incidents to Growing-stage designs, finds six signals in 2026 and defers the Group stage to the 2029 review because no stage-4 signal is planned for 2027–2028.
believe: A stage is a shape, not a revenue number.
Most incidents at a stage are designs from the stage before still running; the leftover, not the missing tool, is what fails.
Two transition signals in one year mean the stage has changed, whatever the revenue says.
can_do: Place a merchant on the map by its channels and stock locations and list which stage each of its systems was bought for.
Sort a program's decisions into those for the current stage, those left from the last one and those copied from a larger company, and say for a group which capabilities to share.

audience.who: Newcomers to commerce architecture; most of all the engineering lead or architect who, like Noor Visser, inherits systems bought at earlier stages and must explain to a board which decisions belong to the company it is now. Product managers and consultants who need to read a vendor's price list as a map of expectations are the second readers.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.

Kestrel & Pine, its people, its ten incidents of 2026 and early 2027 in outline (among them the Black Friday Oversell, the Three-Status Order, the Price Drift, the ASN Chargeback, the Store Stock Mirage, the App That Wrote Stock and the Deprecated Endpoint) and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the business models and the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group) with Kestrel & Pine's years, the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system (OMS), availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II and III: one owning system per product attribute; prices frozen at order placement; available-to-promise; one order record with an OMS once two of four conditions hold; the monthly match of invoices, payouts and bank lines.

From chapters 41 and 42: W4, stay and surround (keep the shop platform, buy the hubs beside it, own the joins), and migrations moved one seam at a time, named there as the moments a merchant moves from one stage to the next.
does_not_know: Stock location as a counting unit of a stage; GMV; fee cliffs and plan thresholds as transition signals.
The transition-signal rule (two signals in one year) and the three directions of a stage mismatch (too early, too late, sideways).
The Group stage's share-or-separate question and the public group evidence (VF Corporation, Zalando and ABOUT YOU, Jacobs 2020, Uber 2020).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant whose revenue says one stage and whose shape says another, the reader places it by shape and names the decision due, rather than by revenue or by adding a tool.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand with €15M revenue runs a web shop, two stores, wholesale including EDI with one retail chain, and a marketplace, all from one warehouse whose stock its ERP copies to the shop every hour. This year it held its first 'which number is right' meeting and had its first peak-day integration failure. Its board calls it a Growing business. Using only this chapter: which stage is it in, and what should it decide first?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Omnichannel by shape: stores, wholesale by EDI and a marketplace sell from one stock, and revenue bands are only markers; it has at least three transition signals this year (an EDI request, two order counts, a first peak integration failure), and two in a year mean the stage has changed. The first decision is which Growing-stage leftovers to retire, not which tool to add: the hourly ERP-to-shop copy and the ERP as stock hub give way to a system of record per fact, availability computed from stock events, an order hub and integration standards with owners, contracts, idempotency and reconciliation. Copying a Group-stage architecture would be The Giant's Boots.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a group adding a brand, the reader decides capability by capability what to share, rather than one stack or full separation.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A group acquires a second outdoor brand that runs its own stack. Using only this chapter: which capabilities should the group share, which may stay separate, and how should it proceed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Always share the integration layer and data definitions, peak tooling, security and compliance, and the PSP contract and fraud rules (with separate merchant accounts where legal entities require). Share the storefront when the brands are positioned alike, keep it separate when brand identity is the product; share the attribute model in a PIM with brand workspaces; share stock and availability when warehouses serve both brands; share the order hub when customers buy across brands. An acquisition turns the question into sequencing, which is a migration. Forcing one stack by decree, or keeping everything apart, without measuring the benefit is One Size Fits None; autonomy without shared standards produces the Spaghetti Junction at group scale.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why a merchant's current-stage incidents are attributed to the stage before, and what that changes in its program.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Kestrel & Pine's incidents of 2026 and early 2027 happened while it was an Omnichannel business. Using only this chapter: why does the stage map attribute most of them to the Growing stage, and what follows for Waypoint?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Eight of the ten incidents trace to designs from 2019–2022 still running in 2026: the hourly stock sync built when marketplace orders were a few a day, agency scripts written for one channel at a time, the ERP as hub for stock it did not hold, and the nightly POS sync from when there was one store. The company had moved stage and the architecture had not. So Waypoint's €1.1M buys the Omnichannel stage's hubs and standards (OMS, PIM, availability service, integration standards) and retires the Growing-stage chain, and it defers Group-stage questions to the 2029 review because no second brand, fourth country or revenue past about €200M is planned for 2027–2028.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That a first store, wholesale customer, marketplace or second brand changes what systems must coordinate (stock in two places) before volume becomes a problem; that the book's four stages, Starting, Growing, Omnichannel and Group, are brought together in one map to recognize transitions, not to copy a larger company's system list; that the stages rest on common practice, dated vendor evidence and the fictional example and are not validated revenue thresholds; that Eva's order crosses products bought at different stages, each with its original assumptions; that a stage is a shape, that leftovers from the previous stage cause the incidents, and that signals arrive before the architecture changes. Evidence: Kestrel & Pine's stage map and priced path, vendor pricing pages and thresholds, and dated public reports of groups.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: Which architecture decisions change as a business grows, and what are the signs that a stage is ending?
thesis.claim: A scale stage is a shape (the channels that sell, the locations that hold stock), not a revenue band. Each stage moves the order record, stock record and integration style to a system that owns each fact, and retires the previous stage's systems, which still run on its assumptions. A stage is ending when two signals of a new shape, such as a second stock location or a connector nobody owns, arrive in one year.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a business grows along a revenue line and its architecture should be scaled up when volume demands it: buy the systems that companies in the next revenue band use, and keep what works until it breaks under load.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim places itself by shape, retires the previous stage's leftovers before adding tools, and sorts each decision by the stage it belongs to. Kestrel & Pine's April 2027 stage map found it had been in the Omnichannel stage since 2023, attributed eight of its ten incidents to Growing-stage designs still running in 2026, counted six transition signals in 2026, and deferred Group-stage questions to the 2029 review because none of their signals (a second brand, a fourth country, revenue past about €200M) is planned for 2027–2028. Waypoint, its 2027 improvement program, spends €1.1M on the Omnichannel hubs and retires the hourly chain. The fee cliff that matters most to it is payments, not the platform plan: on €27.0M of online revenue each half percentage point of payment cost is about €135,000 a year.
thesis.how_why: Each channel or stock location added multiplies the systems that must agree about the same stock, order and product facts, so the same fact must travel faster and more reliably at each stage: from the platform's own count, to a scheduled copy from the ERP, to an availability service fed by stock events. Systems are bought when a channel arrives, by whoever is available, with that moment's assumptions (one store, a few marketplace orders a day), and because they keep working nobody retires them; under the next stage's load the assumption fails at the join. Vendors tier their prices on volume and shape, so fee cliffs and plan thresholds mark a transition before an incident does. Each signal is either a new channel or stock location the existing joins were not built for, or a join already slipping (a connector without an owner, two counts of one fact); one can be a one-off, but two in one year (the author's rule) mean the channels and the joins have both changed.

supporting_claims.claim: A scale stage is a shape of business (how many channels sell and how many locations hold stock, and at the Group stage how many brands or units share them), not a revenue band; revenue bands are only markers, and vendors' price tiers and fee cliffs mark the same shape changes.

At each stage the order record, the stock record and the integration style move toward a hub that owns each fact, because the same fact must reach more systems faster and more reliably: the platform's own count, then a scheduled copy, then an availability service fed by events.

Systems are bought for the stage the business is in and keep running into the next one; those leftovers are where the next stage's incidents come from (eight of Kestrel & Pine's ten), so the decision at a transition is which leftovers to retire, and a stage mismatch fails too early, too late or sideways.

The signals of a transition (a fee cliff, a second stock location, an EDI request, two order counts, an unowned connector, a first peak-day integration failure, a second brand) arrive before the incidents, and two in one year mean the stage has changed.
At the Group stage the question is no longer which systems but which are shared, answered capability by capability with conditions, because forcing one stack and keeping everything apart both fail.

role.contribution: Gives the part its rule about timing: one map of the four stages, the signals that a stage is ending and the Group stage's share-or-separate table, with Kestrel & Pine's April 2027 stage map tracing its incidents to leftovers from the stage before.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene: the board's question and the stage map's answer, which the chapter then generalizes
stages and practice: the stages in the order a business meets them, and Kestrel & Pine's path from 2016 to 2027

flow.rationale: The scene ('Setting the Scene') gives the board's question and the stage map's uncomfortable row, so the reader knows what the chapter must explain. 'What a Scale Stage Is' defines the unit the map is drawn in; 'The Map' then sets all four stages side by side before any is examined, and 'How Fresh Must a Fact Be?' explains the map's main movement (records moving to hubs) by the requirement behind it. 'Stage by Stage' goes from the whole to each part, in the order a business meets the stages, and its Group section raises the share-or-separate question that 'The Group's Decision Table' answers next to it. 'The Transition Signals' gathers the ending signals each stage named into one table and the two-signal rule, which needs every stage told first. 'In Practice' prices one merchant's whole path, which needs the stages and signals; 'When It Goes Wrong' comes last because each direction of failure (too early, too late, sideways) is read against the stages and the table. Putting 'How Fresh Must a Fact Be?' after the stage sections would leave the map's movement toward hubs unexplained while each stage relies on it; folding the decision table into the Group stage's section would bury the chapter's one recommendation table among the evidence. Putting the map after 'Stage by Stage' would leave the stage sections without the frame they fill in; putting the signals before the stages would list endings of stages not yet described; putting 'In Practice' first would price leftovers the reader cannot yet place.

hook.content: A merchant opens its first store while still selling online: the servers have room to spare, but stock now sits in two places and either channel may fulfill an order, so systems built for one warehouse must coordinate decisions they were never designed for.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has watched a small business add a shop, a wholesale customer or a marketplace knows that the work changes before the volume does.
bridge.to_topic: Chapter 42's migrations are how a merchant crosses from one such shape to the next; the stages themselves say which decisions each shape makes necessary and how to see the next one coming.

Two transition signals in one year mean a stage is ending.

sections.heading: What a Scale Stage Is, and Is Not

sections.heading: Stage by Stage

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the Growing stage fees change character (the third-party gateway fee, per-order tool prices, open-source plans paid above €1 million GMV), and a merchant moving to Omnichannel crosses several thresholds at once, so price lists are a transition signal.

evidence.what: Shopify gateway fee 2% on Basic; Picqer €379 a month including 3,000 orders, then €0.28 an order (accessed November 2026); Shopware's €1M GMV line.
evidence.shows: Fee changes mark the transition.
evidence.source: Shopify, Picqer and Shopware pricing pages

transition_in.carries_over: The joins the Growing stage accretes.
transition_in.introduces: The fees it starts to meet.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Growing stage ends on concrete signals: a retail chain asks for EDI (still most of European B2B electronic ordering by value), a second stock location must be sold from, two reports show two order counts, and the first peak day's failure is in an integration, followed closely by an unowned connector, support opening several systems and an app writing another system's fact; the EDI request often comes first because European B2B electronic ordering is still mostly EDI by value.

evidence.what: Eurostat 2024 data (extracted February 2026): EDI-type sales 11.07% of EU enterprise turnover against 8.39% for web sales.
evidence.shows: A wholesale line meets EDI before a B2B web shop.

transition_in.carries_over: The Growing stage's joins and fees.
transition_in.introduces: The signals that it is ending.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At the Omnichannel stage three or four business models share one stock, and for a retailer with stores omnichannel is the business, with an order hub what makes store stock sellable online.

evidence.what: Target's 10-K for fiscal 2025 (filed March 2026): stores fulfilled 97.6% of merchandise sales.
evidence.shows: Store stock is the online business's stock.

transition_in.carries_over: The end of the Growing stage.
transition_in.introduces: The Omnichannel stage's shape.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: What becomes necessary at the Omnichannel stage is Waypoint's set: a system of record per fact, an OMS, a PIM, an availability service and integration standards with owner, contract, idempotency and reconciliation, with the ERP demoted from hub.

evidence.what: Akeneo guidance (accessed November 2026): content scattered across teams, manual channel launches and inconsistent storefront data signal a PIM.
evidence.shows: Vendor guidance places the PIM at this stage (vendor content).

transition_in.introduces: The decisions it makes necessary.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Omnichannel stage's temptation is The Giant's Boots: public examples come from companies with hundreds of engineers, so a 14-person team should adopt composable per capability around a kept core and own the joins.

evidence.what: Fowler, MonolithFirst (June 2015): boundaries are hard to get right at the beginning; Shopify Engineering (February 2019): a modular monolith for over a thousand developers; MACH Alliance survey (February 2026): 37% of 600 cite integration complexity.
evidence.shows: Even the advocates' evidence warns against copying a large company's style.

transition_in.introduces: What it is tempted to copy instead.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Omnichannel stage ends with a second brand or unit, an acquisition, a fourth country with its own books, or the platform's tenancy binding; a vendor's enterprise band of $50 million to $500 million of GMV hints at the stage's top.

evidence.what: Shopify enterprise page (accessed November 2026): organizations with GMV of $50M to $500M and more.
evidence.shows: The nearest public hint of where a vendor sees the top of this stage.

transition_in.carries_over: The Omnichannel stage's needs and temptation.
transition_in.introduces: The signals that it is ending.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Group stage is defined by plurality (several brands, units or countries that could each run a stack), so its question becomes which systems are shared and who owns them.

transition_in.carries_over: The end of the Omnichannel stage.
transition_in.introduces: The Group stage's shape and question.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: VF Corporation's direct-to-consumer business across brand stores and sites, 44% of revenue, shows one group with many brand storefronts and a shared question about what sits behind them.

evidence.what: VF Corporation 10-K for the fiscal year to March 2026: DTC across brands such as The North Face and Timberland, 44% of revenue.
evidence.shows: Many brand storefronts in one group.

transition_in.introduces: A multi-brand group that faces it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An acquisition changes a group's metrics on day one and its architecture over years, as Zalando's consolidation of ABOUT YOU diluted its reported partner share before any system was touched.

evidence.what: Zalando Annual Report 2025 (March 2026): partner-business share of GMV fell to 32.1% from 34.2% by dilution after consolidating ABOUT YOU.
evidence.shows: The numbers change before the systems.

transition_in.introduces: What an acquisition does first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Group stage's failure pattern is One Size Fits None (one stack forced without measuring, or shareable work duplicated), and the public cautions against too much autonomy, Zalando's services in six languages and Uber's 2,200 microservices, are six years old and from far larger companies, but the lesson transfers: autonomy without shared standards produces the Spaghetti Junction at group scale.

evidence.what: Jacobs 2020: more than 260 teams, similar services 'written in six languages', which 'hurts productivity at scale'; Uber 2020: about 2,200 microservices, an investigation through fifty services owned by twelve teams.
evidence.shows: Autonomy without standards is costly at scale; both sources flagged as old.

transition_in.carries_over: Groups that must decide what to share, seen in VF and Zalando.
transition_in.introduces: The failure pattern of that decision and the evidence of what too much autonomy costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Group stage's remaining questions are vendor-scale ones (tenancy, extensibility, data residency, exit terms), and the Data Act's ban on switching charges from 12 January 2027 may or may not reach hosted commerce platforms; the main question, which capabilities to share, is left to the decision table that follows.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854: switching charges for data processing services prohibited from 12 January 2027; whether hosted commerce platforms fall under it is open as of November 2026.
evidence.shows: Exit terms become a group-level contract question.

transition_in.carries_over: What a group shares and what it keeps apart.
transition_in.introduces: The vendor-scale questions left.

sections.heading: Multi-Brand and Multi-Country: The Group's Decision Table
sections.controlling_idea: The Group stage's question is answered capability by capability: share the integration layer, data definitions, peak tooling, security and the PSP contract always, and share storefront, PIM, stock and the order hub only under stated conditions; acquisitions turn the question into a migration.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the share-or-separate decision per capability with its conditions.

transition_in.carries_over: The Group stage's question of what to share.
transition_in.introduces: The answer per capability.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's default shares expensive capabilities with common requirements, run once by a platform team, and leaves brand-visible ones with the brands; the decision table says, per capability, when to share across brands or units and when to keep separate: always share the PSP contract and fraud rules, the integration layer and data definitions, peak tooling, security and compliance; share storefront, PIM, stock and the order hub under conditions.

evidence.what: Seven capabilities with 'share when' and 'keep separate when' conditions; separate definitions of 'order' per brand named as the Group-stage Schrödinger's Order.
evidence.shows: The question is settled per capability, not for the whole stack.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two conditions govern the table: an acquired brand brings its own stack, so the question becomes sequencing, which is a migration; and a group that runs a marketplace or partner program has become a platform vendor with its tenancy concerns.

transition_in.introduces: The two conditions that change how it is applied.

sections.heading: The Transition Signals
sections.controlling_idea: Each transition signal was visible at Kestrel & Pine before the incident that priced it, and two signals in one year mean the stage has changed, whatever the revenue says.

advances_thesis.how: Maps each signal to what it means, the pattern it precedes and Kestrel & Pine's case, and states the two-signal rule.

transition_in.carries_over: The signals named for each stage in turn and the Group stage's question.
transition_in.introduces: All the signals in one table, with the pattern each precedes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table gathers the ending signals each stage section named, and every signal that led to an incident was visible at Kestrel & Pine before the incident that priced it: a fee threshold, a second stock location, an EDI request, two order counts, an unowned connector, support opening several systems, an app writing another system's fact, a peak-day integration failure, and the not-yet second brand.

evidence.what: Nine signals with what each means, the pattern it precedes and Kestrel & Pine's case (enterprise tier 2023; Duiven 2023; Bergzicht 2025 and the ASN Chargeback; three definitions of 'order'; the Deprecated Endpoint; the Three-Status Order; the App That Wrote Stock; Black Friday 2026; not yet).
evidence.shows: Signals arrive before incidents.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's rule is that two signals in one year mean the stage has changed, whatever the revenue says; Kestrel & Pine had six in 2026 (stores selling online stock, the ASN Chargeback, the App That Wrote Stock, the Three-Status Order, the Black Friday integration failure, three definitions of order), signals that marked its 2023 change of shape long before the April 2027 stage map named it.

evidence.what: Figure 4: transitions triggered by shape changes, with self-loops where a stage does its work.
evidence.shows: Shape, not revenue, moves a business between stages.

transition_in.introduces: The rule for reading them.

sections.heading: In Practice: Kestrel & Pine's Path, Priced
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's path from 2016 to 2027, priced from its own figures, shows a Starting stage that left a habit, a Growing stage whose joins caused eight of the ten incidents, an Omnichannel stage whose incidents cost about €138,000 directly, a payment fee worth more than all of them, and a 2027 stage map that sorts decisions by shape.

advances_thesis.how: Prices the leftovers and the fee cliff for one merchant.

flow.rationale: The stages in Kestrel & Pine's own order, then the fee example that the Omnichannel costs make comparable, then the 2027 stage map that the whole path leads to.

transition_in.carries_over: The signals and the two-signal rule.
transition_in.introduces: One merchant's whole path, with costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The stage map is more persuasive with costs, so the section gives Kestrel & Pine's figures with one illustrative calculation.
Kestrel & Pine's Starting stage (2016–2018) was the vendor's architecture and caused no 2026 incident, except the habit that the agency owns the storefront.

evidence.what: One Dutch web shop on the shop platform, one PSP, a 3PL in Tiel, an agency from 2017.
evidence.shows: The Starting stage left a habit, not a system failure.

transition_in.introduces: The first stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Its Growing stage (2019–2022) built every join when its channel arrived, and eight of the ten incidents descend from that era's designs, the clearest being the Store Stock Mirage, the Deprecated Endpoint and the Black Friday Oversell's cadence.

evidence.what: Arnhem store and nightly POS sync (2019), Belgium (2020), Utrecht, connector, iPaaS, GTINs (2021), Germany, investor, Ruben Alves (2022); the Store Stock Mirage (37 items), the Deprecated Endpoint.
evidence.shows: The incidents trace to this era's joins.

transition_in.introduces: The Growing stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Its Omnichannel stage (2023–2026) brought thirteen systems, four order records, four copies of stock and three definitions of 'order', technology spend of about €2.6 million (5.4% of revenue, high against a judged 2–4%), and incidents with about €138,000 of direct cost.

evidence.what: €2.6M, 5.4% of revenue; €96,000 (Oversell), €19,400 refunded twice, €8,200 (Price Drift), €14,200 (ASN Chargeback): about €138,000.
evidence.shows: What the leftovers cost one merchant.

transition_in.introduces: The Omnichannel stage and its costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The fee cliff that matters most to Kestrel & Pine is payments, not the €2,300-a-month platform tier: on €27.0 million of online revenue each half point of payment cost is about €135,000 a year, nearly as much as the four priced incidents and recurring every year.

evidence.what: 0.5% × €27.0M ≈ €135,000 a year (illustrative arithmetic on ledger figures); enterprise tier €2,300 a month.
evidence.shows: The PSP contract is an architecture decision.

transition_in.introduces: A fee that outweighs them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2027 the stage map lets Waypoint's €1.1 million buy the Omnichannel stage's hubs and standards, retire the Growing stage's chain and defer the Group stage: the stages sort decisions by the shape they belong to.

evidence.what: Waypoint, €1.1M over 2027–2028; Group stage deferred to the 2029 review.
evidence.shows: The stages are used to sort decisions, not to predict revenue.

transition_in.introduces: What the 2027 stage map does with them.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong: Too Early, Too Late, Sideways
sections.controlling_idea: A stage mismatch fails too early (The Giant's Boots), too late (The Phantom Stock, Schrödinger's Order) or sideways (One Size Fits None), each with a detection and a recovery, and every recovery runs through an entity–owner table and a reconciliation job per copy.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the three directions in which decisions taken for the wrong stage fail, and how each is detected and recovered.

flow.rationale: The three directions in the order of a business's growth (ahead of its stage, behind it, then across a group), then the two tools all three recoveries share.

transition_in.carries_over: Kestrel & Pine's path, where decisions were sorted by stage.
transition_in.introduces: What happens when they are not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A stage mismatch fails in three directions, each with a detection and a recovery.

Too early, a Growing-stage merchant adopts a composable core or microservices from larger companies' case studies; it shows when the integration layer is the largest effort and nobody is on call, and it is recovered by consolidating, as Segment did.

evidence.what: Segment (2018) folded more than 140 services back into one (its own account, eight years old).
evidence.shows: Consolidation is a known recovery.

transition_in.introduces: The first: too early.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Too late, an Omnichannel merchant runs Growing-stage copies; one reconciliation detects it cheaply, as Kestrel & Pine's May 2027 count of 2.3% differing variants did, and Waypoint's hubs, events and kept reconciliation are the recovery.

evidence.what: First weekly reconciliation, May 2027: 2.3% of active variants with a different quantity, most from the apps that wrote stock.
evidence.shows: The leftover shows up as soon as someone counts.

transition_in.introduces: Moving too late.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Sideways, a group forces one stack or keeps everything apart without measuring; it shows as consolidation with no per-capability benefit or as many definitions of 'customer', and the decision table applied per capability is the recovery.

transition_in.introduces: The third direction: sideways, at the Group stage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every recovery runs through an entity–owner table and a reconciliation job per copy; the stage sets how many rows those tools have, not whether they are needed.

transition_in.introduces: What they share.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The first store, Eva's order across systems from four different years and Kestrel & Pine's incidents are one fact seen three times: a stage changes when the shape of the business changes, and the systems bought for the old shape keep running until someone decides to retire them. The stage map turns that into a decision rule: place the business by shape, retire the previous stage's leftovers, and wait for the next stage's signals before buying for it.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant that asks which shape it has and which stage each system was bought for can tell a board which decisions are due now, which are leftovers and which belong to a larger company; revenue answers none of these. Kestrel & Pine spends Waypoint's €1.1 million on its own stage and leaves the Group stage to the 2029 review.

callback.to: The introduction's merchant that opens a first store and has stock in two places, and Eva's order crossing systems bought in 2016, 2021, 2023 and 2025.
callback.how: Paragraph p53 reads both as changes of shape whose systems were never retired, and names the eight of ten incidents that followed at Kestrel & Pine.

takeaway.content: Place the business by shape, list which stage each system was bought for, and ask the eight questions: the stage by shape, the vendor thresholds ahead, the stock writers, the order records, the integrations' owners, last year's signals, what a second brand would share, and which current decisions belong to which stage.

hand_off.carries_over: The stage map's sorting of decisions by stage, including its row on who builds and runs at each stage.
hand_off.introduces: The people who make and keep the decisions: who owns each system, integration and app, how a fourteen-person team works with an agency and a dozen vendors, and governance that fits a merchant.

transition_in.carries_over: The three ways a stage mismatch fails and the two tools that recover them.
transition_in.introduces: What the chapter establishes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The opening's first store and Eva's order are changes of shape whose systems were never retired: Kestrel & Pine had been an Omnichannel business since 2023 while eight of its ten incidents came from Growing-stage designs, so Waypoint retires them and leaves the Group stage to its signals; a merchant asks which shape it has and which stage each system was bought for, which revenue cannot answer.

evidence.what: The hook's first store, Eva's order across systems from 2016 to 2025, the eight of ten incidents, Waypoint's €1.1 million and the 2029 review.
evidence.shows: The chapter's answer applies to the opening's cases.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: vendors tier on volume and shape; by value European B2B electronic ordering is still mostly EDI; for a retailer with stores omnichannel fulfillment is the business; and autonomy without shared standards is costly at group scale.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's answer in one paragraph.
transition_in.introduces: The points that are established.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Depends on context: whether an OMS, PIM or WMS is needed (channel and location counts, not volume), how to read revenue bands, when the ERP as hub stops working, and what a group shares.

transition_in.introduces: What depends on the merchant's situation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's synthesis: the first decision at each stage is which leftovers to retire; and two transition signals in one year mean the stage has changed, so a stage map that lists the signals is worth more to a board than a roadmap of tools.

transition_in.carries_over: What is established and what depends on context.
transition_in.introduces: The author's own judgement, labeled as such.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eight questions let the reader apply the map: the stage by shape and each system's stage, the vendor thresholds ahead, the stock writers and comparisons, the order records, the integrations' builders and owners, last year's signals, what a second brand would share, and which current decisions belong to which stage.

transition_in.introduces: Questions that apply them to the reader's own business.
